# Microbes and their hosts

> *Most people carry potential pathogens without harm, yet the same organism can make one person ill
> and leave another well. Whether disease follows, and whether the damage comes from the microbe or
> from the host's own response, depends on properties of both.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish contamination, colonisation, infection and disease, and define a carrier.
- Explain how the resident microbiota protects the host, and what follows when it is disturbed.
- Relate each major gap in host defence to the kind of organism it allows to cause disease.
- Place a pathogen on the range from opportunistic to primary, and name the opportunities an
  opportunist needs.
- Describe the steps of infection, and distinguish exotoxins from endotoxin.
- Use the damage-response framework to judge whether damage comes mainly from the microbe, the host
  response, or both.
:::

## States of the encounter {#sec-host-words}

Four terms describe how far an encounter between a microbe and a host has progressed. They are often
used interchangeably, although each describes a different state.

| Term | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Contamination | Microbes are present on a surface but not multiplying | Bacteria on an unwashed hand |
| Colonisation | Microbes live and multiply at a site without causing damage | *Staphylococcus aureus* in the nose of a healthy person |
| Infection | Microbes multiply in tissue, and the host responds | Bacteria multiplying in a wound, with local inflammation |
| Disease | The host is damaged enough to produce signs and symptoms | Fever, pain and swelling from that wound |

Infection does not always lead to disease. A person who harbours and can transmit an organism without
being ill is a **carrier**.

::: {.example}
About a fifth of healthy people carry *S. aureus* in the nose persistently, and can pass it on by
hand, without being ill [@kluytmans1997carriage].
:::

## The host {#sec-host-host}

### The resident microbiota {#sec-host-microbiota}

The **microbiota** is the community of microbes that normally lives on and in the body: in the colon,
the mouth, the skin, the upper airway and the vagina. Most of these organisms are **commensals**,
which live on a host without harming it. The composition of the microbiota differs between sites
because each site offers different conditions: stomach acid, the dryness and salt of skin, and the
near-absence of oxygen in the colon each select for different organisms.

Resident microbes contribute to defence and to nutrition in several ways:

- They occupy attachment sites and consume nutrients that incoming organisms would need, a protection
  called **colonisation resistance**.
- Some produce substances that inhibit competitors.
- Their presence helps the immune system develop and stay regulated.
- Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre the host cannot digest, and synthesise vitamin K and several B
  vitamins.

Disturbing the community removes this protection, and an organism that the disturbance spares can
multiply in place of the residents.

::: {.example}
Antibacterial drugs do not act on fungi. A course of antibacterial treatment can therefore reduce the
vaginal bacteria and allow the yeast *Candida albicans* to overgrow.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "microbes are germs, and germs are harmful"
Children as young as seven describe microorganisms as essentially harmful [@byrne2011children], and
the idea persists into adult life. Pathogens are in fact a small minority, and many common bacterial
infections are caused by organisms that also live on people harmlessly. *Escherichia coli*, for
example, lives harmlessly in the gut but causes infection when it reaches the bladder. What usually
changes is the site the organism reaches, or the state of the host.
:::

### Host factors {#sec-host-factors}

When two people meet the same organism and only one becomes ill, the reasons usually lie with the
host. Casadevall and Pirofski group them under the mnemonic **MISTEACHING**: Microbiota, Inoculum,
Sex, Temperature, Environment, Age, Chance, History of exposure, Immunity, Nutrition and Genetics
[@casadevall2018misteaching]. Two of these factors account for most differences between patients.

The **inoculum**, the number of organisms received, affects both whether disease follows and how
quickly it begins: for some organisms ten to a hundred cells are enough, while for others a million or
more must be swallowed.

**Immunity** includes the specific immunity left by earlier exposure or vaccination and the general
competence of the defences. Each gap in the defences allows a particular kind of organism to cause
disease:

::: {.concept-tree}
[Gaps in host defence and the organisms they let through]{.tree-title}

- Defences impaired
  - **Neutropenia**, a low neutrophil count, as after chemotherapy: bacteria and fungi, such as
    *C. albicans*
  - Impaired cell-mediated immunity, as in advanced HIV infection: organisms that live inside host
    cells, such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*
  - **Asplenia**, absence of a functioning spleen: bacteria with a polysaccharide capsule
  - Diabetes, which impairs neutrophil function: several bacteria, such as *Burkholderia
    pseudomallei*
:::

::: {.example}
**Melioidosis** is infection with *B. pseudomallei*, a bacterium of soil and surface water. In
Singapore, more than half of patients with melioidosis had diabetes, about three times the proportion
in the general population of similar age [@pang2018melioidosis].
:::

## The microbe {#sec-host-microbe}

### Virulence {#sec-host-opportunism}

**Virulence** is the degree to which an organism can cause disease. Pathogens are commonly divided by
virulence into **opportunistic pathogens**, which cause disease only when the host's defences are
impaired or when they reach a site they do not normally occupy, and **primary** (or strict)
**pathogens**, which cause disease in people with normal defences. The two groups are the ends of a
continuous range.

::: {.spectrum}
[Host defence that must fail before disease occurs]{.tree-title}

- *C. albicans*: disease mainly when defences fail
- *S. aureus*: colonises healthy people; disease when it crosses a barrier
- *M. tuberculosis*: disease in people with normal defences

[Opportunistic pathogen]{.spectrum-end} [Primary pathogen]{.spectrum-end}
:::

An opportunistic pathogen gets its opportunity in one of three ways:

1. A barrier is breached: skin is cut, a catheter crosses it, or surgery lets gut organisms into the
   peritoneal cavity.
2. Defences are weakened ([host factors](#sec-host-factors)).
3. The microbiota is disturbed ([the resident microbiota](#sec-host-microbiota)).

Because the boundary between the groups is not sharp, the damage-response framework replaces them with
a single measure: how much damage an organism causes in a particular host (see [Source of the
damage](#sec-host-drf)).

### Steps of infection {#sec-host-steps}

To cause an infection, a microbe has to complete a sequence of steps. Anything it uses to complete
them is a **virulence factor**: a product or structure that helps it infect or damage a host.

::: {.flow}
1. Attach to a surface
2. Invade, or act from the surface
3. Evade defences
4. Obtain nutrients
5. Damage the host
:::

Iron is the nutrient most often in short supply, because the host keeps it bound to proteins. Damage,
the last step, can be done by the microbe directly or by the response it provokes.

Attachment explains **tropism**, the range of tissues or cells an organism can occupy. A microbe can
settle only where it finds the molecule it binds.

::: {.example}
Influenza virus binds a receptor carried by cells lining the airway, so it infects the airway and not
the skin.
:::

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/pathogenesis-sorter.yml"></div>

### Toxins {#sec-host-toxins}

Two different kinds of molecule are called toxins. **Exotoxins** are proteins that bacteria secrete.
**Endotoxin** is lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a structural part of the Gram-negative outer membrane
(see [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope)).

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-exotoxin-endotoxin.yml"></div>

Because exotoxins are proteins, they can be inactivated and used as **toxoid** vaccines. LPS cannot,
and the inflammation it drives causes much of the shock in severe Gram-negative infection.

## The outcome {#sec-host-outcome}

### Source of the damage {#sec-host-drf}

The **damage-response framework** of Casadevall and Pirofski defines disease by host damage, and holds
that damage can come from the microbe, from the host's response, or from both
[@casadevall2003damage].

| Main source of damage | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| The microbe | Destruction of host cells; toxins | *C. albicans* multiplying unchecked in a person with neutropenia |
| The host response | Excessive inflammation; immune reactions against the host's own tissue | *S. aureus* toxic shock syndrome, in which a toxin activates a large fraction of T cells at once; rheumatic fever after *Streptococcus pyogenes* infection, in which antibodies cross-react with heart tissue |
| Both | Microbial growth and the response to it, varying with the strength of the response | *M. tuberculosis*: spreads when the response is weak, destroys lung tissue when it is strong |

If damage is plotted against the strength of the host response, different organisms give differently
shaped curves.

<div data-island="damage-response" data-src="/diagrams/damage-response.yml"></div>

On the right-hand side of these curves, damage rises as the immune response grows stronger. General
pathology made the same point about inflammation, which clears an infection but damages tissue when it
is excessive or prolonged. Where most of the damage comes from the host's response, two consequences
follow: a weakened host may show less visible disease, and removing the organism alone may not stop
the damage.

### Time course {#sec-host-courses}

Infections differ in how they unfold over time, and the pattern often follows from the organism's
strategy.

| Pattern | What happens | Typical strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | Rapid onset and a short course | Rapid multiplication and transmission before an immune response develops |
| Latent | The organism persists silently and can reactivate | Survival inside cells, or in a site the immune response reaches poorly |
| Chronic | Infection and inflammation continue for months or years | Resistance to clearance; damage accumulates from the ongoing response |

::: {.example}
*M. tuberculosis* can persist for years in a contained, latent infection and reactivate when immunity
falls, for example in advanced HIV infection.
:::
